name: Decision Fatigue
description: The quality of decisions degrades after a long sequence of decisions, as if decision-making capacity were a depletable resource -- distinct from Ego Depletion's broader willpower-resource claim, this is specifically about decision-making quality declining with decision volume.
design_relevance_note: Invoked to justify limiting choices late in a flow, simplifying settings screens, and sequencing high-stakes decisions (pricing tiers, permissions) earlier rather than later in a session -- but the flagship real-world evidence for this exact effect is seriously disputed, so design teams citing it as settled science are overstating the case.
myth_risk_note: The single most-cited real-world demonstration of this exact concept has a specific, credible, statistical counter-explanation that requires no decision-fatigue mechanism at all -- a genuine, documented dispute, not a settled finding, even though the term is used in product discourse as if it were established science.
prevalence_note: A commonly invoked justification in product/UX discourse for limiting choices, simplifying settings, and sequencing decisions within a flow, even though the term is rarely traced back to its actual (disputed) evidentiary basis.

findings.description: Analyzing over 1,000 parole decisions made by 8 experienced Israeli judges over 50 days, the probability of a favorable ruling dropped from roughly 65% at the start of a session to nearly 0% by its end — then jumped back to roughly 65% immediately after each of the judges' two daily food breaks. Interpreted as evidence that mental depletion ('decision fatigue') from a sequence of consecutive decisions degrades judgment quality, even in high-stakes professional contexts.
findings.effect_size: favorable rulings ~65% at session start, declining to ~0% by session end, returning to ~65% after a break
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

findings.description: Computational simulations showed the dramatic session-order effect Danziger et al. reported can be fully explained by a statistical artifact: favorable rulings simply take longer to process than unfavorable ones, so judges naturally end up skipping the longer, favorable-leaning cases right before a scheduled break — no actual decline in judgment quality is required to produce the same pattern. A hypothetical judge who plans ahead only minimally would produce an effect of similar magnitude.
findings.source_title: The Irrational Hungry Judge Effect Revisited: Simulations Reveal That the Magnitude of the Effect Is Overestimated

applications.title: Obama wearing only gray or blue suits to eliminate a daily decision
applications.description: As president, Barack Obama deliberately limited his wardrobe to gray or blue suits, explaining in his own words that he was trying to 'pare down decisions' on low-stakes matters (what to eat, what to wear) to preserve mental capacity for higher-stakes presidential decisions -- explicitly citing research that 'the simple act of making decisions degrades one's ability to make further decisions.'
applications.ethical_note: This is a real person's own self-management practice, not a designed influence directed at a third party or user -- there is no persuasive intent to grade here, only a genuine real-world illustration of the underlying phenomenon (decision fatigue depleting a limited resource across a day). Distinct from this graph's typical Application entries, which usually examine a company's choice architecture aimed at users; here the 'user' and the decision-maker are the same person, so no manipulation dimension applies.
